**Caveats**

The `fs.watch` API is not 100% consistent across platforms, and is unavailable in some situations.

On Windows, no events will be emitted if the watched directory is moved or renamed. An `EPERM` error is reported when the watched directory is deleted.

The `fs.watch` API does not provide any protection with respect to malicious actions on the file system. For example, on Windows it is implemented by monitoring changes in a directory versus specific files. This allows substitution of a file and fs reporting changes on the new file with the same filename.

**Availability**

This feature depends on the underlying operating system providing a way to be notified of file system changes.

*   On Linux systems, this uses inotify(7).
*   On BSD systems, this uses kqueue(2).
*   On macOS, this uses kqueue(2) for files and FSEvents for directories.
*   On SunOS systems (including Solaris and SmartOS), this uses event ports.
*   On Windows systems, this feature depends on ReadDirectoryChangesW.
*   On AIX systems, this feature depends on AHAFS, which must be enabled.
*   On IBM i systems, this feature is not supported.

If the underlying functionality is not available for some reason, then `fs.watch()` will not be able to function and may throw an exception. For example, watching files or directories can be unreliable, and in some cases impossible, on network file systems (NFS, SMB, etc) or host file systems when using virtualization software such as Vagrant or Docker.

It is still possible to use `fs.watchFile()`, which uses stat polling, but this method is slower and less reliable.

**Inodes**

On Linux and macOS systems, `fs.watch()` resolves the path to an inode and watches the inode. If the watched path is deleted and recreated, it is assigned a new inode. The watch will emit an event for the delete but will continue watching the _original_ inode. Events for the new inode will not be emitted. This is expected behavior.

AIX files retain the same inode for the lifetime of a file. Saving and closing a watched file on AIX will result in two notifications (one for adding new content, and one for truncation).

**Filename argument**

Providing `filename` argument in the callback is only supported on Linux, macOS, Windows, and AIX. Even on supported platforms, `filename` is not always guaranteed to be provided. Therefore, don't assume that `filename` argument is always provided in the callback, and have some fallback logic if it is `null`.

## Web research: fs.watch caveats

Question: "research what the Node.js docs at https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html say about fs.watch caveats"

### Facts
1. fs.watch does not behave the same on every platform, and in some situations it is unavailable. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "The fs.watch API is not 100% consistent across platforms, and is unavailable in some situations."
2. On Windows, moving or renaming the watched directory produces no events. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "On Windows, no events will be emitted if the watched directory is moved or renamed."
3. On Windows, deleting the watched directory reports an EPERM error. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "An EPERM error is reported when the watched directory is deleted."
4. fs.watch gives no protection against malicious changes to the file system. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "The fs.watch API does not provide any protection with respect to malicious actions on the file system."
5. fs.watch only works if the operating system can send file system change notifications. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "This feature depends on the underlying operating system providing a way to be notified of file system changes."
6. IBM i does not support fs.watch. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "On IBM i systems, this feature is not supported."
7. On AIX, fs.watch needs AHAFS to be enabled. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "On AIX systems, this feature depends on AHAFS, which must be enabled."
8. If the OS feature is missing, fs.watch will not work and may throw an exception. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "If the underlying functionality is not available for some reason, then fs.watch() will not be able to function and may throw an exception."
9. Watching can be unreliable or impossible on network file systems and on host file systems used through Vagrant or Docker. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "...on network file systems (NFS, SMB, etc) or host file systems when using virtualization software such as Vagrant or Docker."
10. The fallback, fs.watchFile, uses stat polling but is slower and less reliable. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "It is still possible to use fs.watchFile(), which uses stat polling, but this method is slower and less reliable."
11. On Linux and macOS, if a watched path is deleted and recreated, the watch keeps following the original inode. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "The watch will emit an event for the delete but will continue watching the original inode."
12. No events are sent for the recreated file's new inode. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "Events for the new inode will not be emitted."
13. On AIX, saving and closing a watched file sends two notifications. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "Saving and closing a watched file on AIX will result in two notifications (one for adding new content, and one for truncation)."
14. The callback only gets a filename argument on Linux, macOS, Windows and AIX. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "Providing filename argument in the callback is only supported on Linux, macOS, Windows, and AIX."
15. Even on those platforms, the filename may be missing, so code needs a fallback for null. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "Even on supported platforms, filename is not always guaranteed to be provided."
16. The recursive option (watching subdirectories) only works on supported platforms. Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "This applies when a directory is specified, and only on supported platforms"
17. The same caveats also apply to fsPromises.watch(). Source: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html "All the caveats for fs.watch() also apply to fsPromises.watch()"

### Inferences
- A sync settings page that relies on fs.watch should say which operating systems it supports, and what the user sees where watching does not work (from facts 1, 5, 6, 7, 8).
- If users can pick a synced folder on a network share or inside a container, live change detection may fail there. The spec needs a defined fallback, such as polling or manual sync, and a message to the user (from facts 9, 10).
- Changes such as moving, renaming, deleting or recreating the synced folder need their own handling, because the watcher can go quiet or report an error (from facts 2, 3, 11, 12).
- Sync logic should not depend on the filename in the event, and should allow for duplicate events (from facts 13, 14, 15).
- Whether subfolders are watched depends on the platform, so a "sync subfolders" setting cannot be assumed to work everywhere (from fact 16).
